Geometrically Consistent Multi-View Scene Generation from Freehand Sketches

Ahmed Bourouis Affiliation: Samsung Research, UK Affiliation: SketchX, University of Surrey, UK
Project Page    Savas Ozkan Affiliation: Samsung Research, UK    Andrea Maracani Affiliation: Samsung Research, UK    Yi-Zhe Song Affiliation: SketchX, University of Surrey, UK
Project Page    Mete Ozay Affiliation: Samsung Research, UK
Abstract

We tackle a new problem: generating geometrically consistent multi-view scenes from a single freehand sketch. Freehand sketches are the most geometrically impoverished input one could offer a multi-view generator. They convey scene intent through abstract strokes while introducing spatial distortions that actively conflict with any consistent 3D interpretation. No prior method attempts this; existing multi-view approaches require photographs or text, while sketch-to-3D methods need multiple views or costly per-scene optimisation.

We address three compounding challenges; absent training data, the need for geometric reasoning from distorted 2D input, and cross-view consistency, through three mutually reinforcing contributions: (i) a curated dataset of ∼\sim9k sketch-to-multiview samples, constructed via an automated generation and filtering pipeline; (ii) Parallel Camera-Aware Attention Adapters (CA3) that inject geometric inductive biases into the video transformer; and (iii) a Sparse Correspondence Supervision Loss (CSL) derived from Structure-from-Motion reconstructions.

Our framework synthesizes all views in a single denoising process without requiring reference images, iterative refinement, or per-scene optimization. Our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art two-stage baselines, improving realism (FID) by over 60% and geometric consistency (Corr-Acc) by 23%, while providing up to a 3.7×\times inference speedup.

Keywords: 
Multi-view synthesis Sketch-based generation Geometric consistency Correspondence supervision

1 Introduction

Consider a rough, freehand sketch of a street scene: a few strokes for a car, some wobbly lines representing buildings, a stick figure on the pavement. Despite this inherent abstraction, a human observer effortlessly infers a plausible 3D world, understanding that the car has an occluded side, the buildings extend beyond the visible corners and the figure could be seen from different perspectives. This rises the fundamental question:

Can a generative model, conditioned solely on a single freehand sketch, synthesize a set of geometrically consistent novel views representative of a complete 3D scene?

We define this task as Sketch-to-Multi-View (S2MV) generation as illustrated in Fig. 1. This task is a surprisingly hard problem for current generative models, and one that has not been studied before. Freehand scene sketches are arguably the most geometrically impoverished conditioning signal one could provide to multiview generators. Unlike photographs, which provide dense appearance and implicit 3D cues (i.e., shading and perspective), or text prompts, which offer semantic flexibility without spatial constrains, freehand sketches are simultaneously spatially informative yet geometrically unreliable. They convey the intent of a scene layout while introducing abstraction, non-linear distortions, and stroke-level noise that often conflict with a consistent 3D interpretation.

Existing multi-view diffusion methods do not directly address these inconsistencies. Image-conditioned approaches [29, 40, 31, 41, 44, 12, 59] typically begin with high-fidelity photographs that already resolve geometric ambiguity. Text-conditioned methods [41] operate in a domain where spatial imprecision is expected and tolerated. Conversely, existing Sketch-to-3D methods, such as Sketch2NeRF [7] and SketchDream [28], are largely restricted to single-object reconstruction or require multiple sketch views and costly per-scene optimisation. To our knowledge, no prior work generates geometrically consistent multi-view outputs from a single, freehand scene sketch.

Bridging this gap requires solving three compounding challenges. (i) Data: no sketch-to-multi-view dataset exists, and freehand sketches cannot be consistently paired with multi-view images through standard rendering pipelines. (ii) Geometric reasoning: generative models must infer coherent 3D structures from a 2D input that lacks strict projective alignment, demanding camera-aware generation mechanisms. (iii) Cross-view consistency: generating different views simultaneously requires the model to enforce correspondences between views, rather than simply conditioning on viewpoint independently.

We address these challenges with the following contributions:

  • •

    A Curation Pipeline for S2MV Data (Sec. 3.2). We introduce a novel pipeline to bridge the domain gap between freehand sketches and multi-view images. By leveraging FS-COCO [9], we synthesize photorealistic frontal views using a pretrained generative model [22], verify sketch-image alignment through semantic segmentation matching [4, 6], and generate multiple views per scene [10]. The resulting dataset includes 9 222 curated samples with 3333 views each, providing a rigorous foundation for S2MV training.

  • •

    Camera-Aware Attention Adapters (CA3) (Sec. 3.3). We propose a lightweight camera attention adapters that inject Projective Rotary Position Encoding (PRoPE) [26] into a pretrained video diffusion transformer [45]. This mechanism adds only 2.7% additional parameters while enabling attention layers to explicitly account for relative projective geometry between views.

  • •

    Correspondance Supervision Loss (CSL) (Sec. 3.4). We introduce a sparse InfoNCE-based correspondence loss applied to the adapter’s latent projections to maintain geometric consistency between cross-views. Using positive pairs extracted through Structure-from-Motion [39],this regularization enforces cross-view identity and merges distinct viewpoints into a unified latent representation.

The components of our framework are mutually reinforcing, creating a cohesive system for S2MV synthesis. While our curated dataset provides the foundational sketch–multiview pairs previously missing from the literature, our CA3 provides the necessary geometric inductive bias and the capacity to reason about viewpoints. Last but not least, our CSL provides the explicit supervisory signal that teaches the model which spatial locations across views should attend to each other, turning geometric capacity into geometric consistency. Removing any one of these components significantly degrades the final performance.

Crucially, our method generates all multi-views jointly in a single end-to-end denoising process directly from a sketch, bypassing any intermediate photo-generation stage, requiring no reference photograph, no per-scene optimisation, no iterative refinement. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first method to produce geometrically coherent, photorealistic multi-view scenes from freehand sketch input.

2 Related Work

Multi-View Generation and Camera Conditioning. Diffusion models have been widely applied to multi-view image generation. Early methods fine-tune image diffusion models to synthesise novel views from a single photograph: Zero-1-to-3 [29] conditions on relative camera pose, and follow-up works [40, 31, 41, 25, 32] improve consistency by generating multiple views jointly through synchronised diffusion or multi-view attention. A parallel line of work repurposes video diffusion models, treating the temporal axis as a viewpoint axis, for object-centric orbiting [44, 8] or scene-level [12] generation. More recent DiT-based architectures push the scale further: Hunyuan3D 2.0 [59] trains a 2B-parameter shape-generation DiT, TRELLIS [51] employs rectified flow transformers over structured 3D latents, and See3D [34] learns 3D priors from 16M video clips without pose annotations.

How camera geometry is communicated to the generative model is a critical design axis. Absolute conditioning methods [29, 13, 50] inject camera parameters as global vectors, while per-pixel Plücker ray representations [13, 53, 60] offer richer spatial encoding but do not inject relative inter-view geometry into the attention computation. Geometric approaches address this limitation directly: PRoPE [26] modulates queries, keys, and values with projective matrices so that attention scores reflect relative camera geometry, UCPE [55] extends this to per-token ray-level encoding, and EpiDiff [16] and SPAD [17] restrict cross-view attention to epipolar lines. AC3D [1] shows that camera information concentrates in a subset of DiT layers, enabling a 4×4{\times} parameter reduction, and the concurrent ReRoPE [24] injects relative pose into underutilised RoPE frequency bands.

We build on the Wan 2.1 video DiT [45] and adopt PRoPE inside lightweight parallel adapters (adding fewer than 3% parameters) following the zero-initialised parallel branch paradigm [56]. We complement the geometric inductive bias with explicit correspondence supervision, a combination not explored in prior work.

Geometric Consistency and Correspondence Supervision. Ensuring cross-view geometric consistency in generated images remains a central challenge. Implicit approaches encode geometric priors through architecture: SyncDreamer [31] constructs a shared 3D feature volume, epipolar attention [16, 25, 42] constrains cross-view attention to geometrically plausible regions, and SpatialCrafter [58] decouples spatial and temporal attention for scene reconstruction. ViewCrafter [54] guides video diffusion with monocular depth-based point clouds, and GeoVideo [2] aligns predicted depth maps across frames during training. In all these cases, geometric reasoning is an emergent property of the architecture rather than an explicitly supervised objective.

In the reconstruction domain, DUSt3R [48], MASt3R [23], and VGGT [47] learn to predict dense correspondences from multi-view images, but treat them as the end product rather than as supervision for generation. CorrespondentDream [18] extracts correspondences from a frozen diffusion UNet to regularise NeRF optimisation, yet does not train the generative model itself with correspondence supervision.

The concurrent CAMEO [21] is closest to our work, supervising attention maps with VGGT-derived correspondences via dense cross-entropy on the main self-attention of a UNet-based model. Our approach differs in two key respects: (i) we use classical SfM correspondences with a sparse InfoNCE [37] contrastive loss and (ii) we supervise lightweight parallel adapters rather than the main attention of a video DiT.

Sketch-Conditioned Generation. Sketch-based image generation has been widely studied through conditional diffusion models. ControlNet [56] and T2I-Adapter [35] accept edge maps as spatial conditions but target clean line drawings rather than freehand sketches. Recent work addresses the sketch abstraction gap: Koley et al. [19] handle amateur sketches for single-image generation, and KnobGen [36] adapts to varying sketch complexity. SketchingReality [3] generates photorealistic images from freehand scene sketches using a CLIP-based sketch encoder, but is limited to single-view output. In the 3D domain, Sketch2NeRF [7] requires multiple sketch views and optimises a NeRF via SDS, while SketchDream [28] combines sketch conditioning with depth guidance, both target single objects and require costly per-scene optimisation.

Our method extends the scene-sketch paradigm of [3] to multi-view output: from a single freehand scene sketch, we generate NN geometrically consistent views through a video diffusion transformer in a single forward pass, with no per-scene optimisation.

3 Method

Given a freehand sketch SS and a set of NN target camera poses, our method generates NN geometrically consistent photorealistic views through a video diffusion transformer (Fig. 2.a) augmented with lightweight camera-aware adapters CA3 (Fig. 2.b) and trained with correspondence supervision CSL(Fig. 2.c).

S2MV requires solving three compounding challenges: the absence of paired training data, the need for camera-aware generation, and the enforcement of cross-view geometric consistency. In this section, we first review the video diffusion backbone (Sec. 3.1), followed by our dataset construction pipeline (Sec. 3.2), Camera-Aware Attention Adapters (CA3) (Sec. 3.3), and Correspondence Supervision Loss (CSL) (Sec. 3.4).

3.1 Preliminaries: Video Diffusion Transformers

Our framework is built upon a standard Video Diffusion Transformer (Wan 2.1 [45]), which is repurposed to support the multi-view sequence modeling required for S2MV. The model operates in a compressed latent space 𝒵\mathcal{Z} learned by a VAE encoder ℰ\mathcal{E}, which first maps a sequence of frames [𝐱i]i=0N[\mathbf{x}_{i}]_{i=0}^{N} into a latent representation [𝐳i]i=0N[\mathbf{z}_{i}]_{i=0}^{N}. Later, the DiT architecture processes each 𝐳i\mathbf{z}_{i} by patchifying it into a sequence of TT tokens whose dimension is DD. Each of the LL transformer blocks computes self-attention as:

Attn​(𝐐,𝐊,𝐕)=softmax​(𝐐𝐊⊤d)​𝐕,\text{Attn}(\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{K},\mathbf{V})=\text{softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\right)\mathbf{V}, (1)

where 𝐐,𝐊,𝐕\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{K},\mathbf{V} are the query, key, and value projections. The training is performed via flow matching [27] by minimizing the velocity field error:

ℒflow=𝔼t,𝐳0,ϵ​[‖𝐯θ​(𝐳t,t,𝐜)−(𝐳0−ϵ)‖2],\mathcal{L}_{\text{flow}}=\mathbb{E}_{t,\mathbf{z}_{0},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left[\|\mathbf{v}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c})-(\mathbf{z}_{0}-\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\|^{2}\right], (2)

where 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t} is the noisy latent at timestep t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}), and 𝐜\mathbf{c} denotes the conditioning signals. The VAE applies 4×4{\times} temporal compression, effective for video where consecutive frames are redundant, but destructive for multi-view generation where neighbouring views differ substantially. We therefore replicate each view four times before encoding (frame replication), yielding 4​N+14N{+}1 input frames and exactly one latent per view.

3.2 Sketch-to-Multiview Dataset Construction

No existing dataset pairs freehand scene sketches with geometrically consistent multi-view images. Unlike photographs, freehand sketches contain non-linear distortions that do not correspond to any standard 3D asset. We therefore propose a pipeline to bridge this domain gap through an automated generation-and-filtering process. The steps in our pipeline are summarized in Fig. 3.

  1. (a)

    Multi-Seed Generation. For each of the ∼{\sim}10,000 sketches in FS-COCO [9], we synthesize five photorealistic candidate images using FLUX.2 dev [22], conditioned on both the sketch and its original caption.

  2. (b)

    Segmentation. To ensure spatial fidelity, we perform semantic grounding by segmenting both the input sketch and the candidates. Sketch masks are extracted via a specialized sketch encoder [4]. For the generated images, we use spaCy to extract object nouns from the caption, which serve as prompts for zero-shot segmentation via GroundingDINO [30] and SAM3 [6].

  3. (c)

    Best Seed Selection. For each sketch, we select the candidate image I∗I^{*} that best aligns with the sketch’s intended spatial layout. This is determined by maximizing the mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU) between the sketch segmentation masks ℳs\mathcal{M}_{s} and the image segmentation masks ℳg\mathcal{M}_{g}:

    I∗=arg⁡maxi∈{1..5}​mIoU​(ℳs,ℳg,i).I^{*}=\arg\max_{i\in\{1..5\}}\text{mIoU}(\mathcal{M}_{s},\mathcal{M}_{g,i}). (3)
  4. (d)

    Multi-View Generation. The selected frontal view is processed by Qwen Image Edit Angles [10] to synthesize NN multi-view images at varying azimuth θ\theta and elevation ϕ\phi.

  5. (e)

    Dataset Curation. We apply a minumum threshold on the mIoU to remove samples where the subjects are poorly aligned.

The result of our pipeline is a final corpus of 9 222 high-quality samples.

3.3 Camera-Aware Attention Adapters (CA3)

A video diffusion model has no intrinsic notion of camera viewpoint as its self-attention treats all tokens identically regardless of their 3D spatial relationship. For photograph-conditioned generation, dense appearance cues in the input can partially compensate; for freehand sketches, which provide only sparse, geometrically distorted strokes, the model receives no implicit 3D signal whatsoever. We therefore equip the model with an explicit geometric inductive bias through lightweight Camera-Aware Attention Adapters (CA3). Below we describe the construction of virtual camera matrices, the projective position encoding that consumes them, the adapter architecture, and a complementary domain-adaptation strategy.

Virtual Camera Matrix Construction. Since our multi-view images are generated via image editing rather than 3D rendering, ground-truth camera parameters are unavailable. We construct virtual cameras by placing each viewpoint on a sphere of fixed radius dd around the scene origin. For a view at azimuth θ\theta and elevation ϕ\phi, we compose a rotation 𝐑(n)=𝐑y​(θ)⋅𝐑x​(ϕ)\mathbf{R}^{(n)}=\mathbf{R}_{y}(\theta)\cdot\mathbf{R}_{x}(\phi) and set the camera position to 𝐭(n)=𝐑(n)​[0,0,d]⊤\mathbf{t}^{(n)}=\mathbf{R}^{(n)}[0,0,d]^{\top}. The camera-to-world extrinsic is then:

𝐓(n)=[𝐑(n)𝐭(n)𝟎⊤1]∈S​E​(3).\mathbf{T}^{(n)}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{R}^{(n)}&\mathbf{t}^{(n)}\\ \mathbf{0}^{\top}&1\end{bmatrix}\in SE(3). (4)

The intrinsic matrix 𝐊\mathbf{K} is shared across all views, constructed from a 60∘60^{\circ} horizontal field-of-view with the principal point at the image centre. These virtual matrices provide CA3 with a consistent geometric coordinate system, enabling viewpoint reasoning in the absence of ground-truth calibration

Viewpoint Awareness via PRoPE. We integrate Projective Rotary Position Encoding (PRoPE) [26], which modulates attention using the scene’s epipolar geometry rather than pixel coordinates alone. For each target view nn, we construct a projective matrix from 𝐓(n)\mathbf{T}^{(n)} and 𝐊\mathbf{K}:

𝐏(n)=[𝐊𝟎𝟎⊤1]⋅(𝐓(n))−1.\mathbf{P}^{(n)}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{K}&\mathbf{0}\\ \mathbf{0}^{\top}&1\end{bmatrix}\cdot(\mathbf{T}^{(n)})^{-1}. (5)

By partitioning the attention head dimensions into projective and spatial subspaces, PRoPE ensures that the affinity between any two tokens is conditioned on their relative projective transform 𝐏(nq)​𝐏(nk)−1\mathbf{P}^{(n_{q})}\mathbf{P}^{(n_{k})^{-1}}, embedding epipolar constraints directly into the attention computation.

CA3 Architecture. To preserve the powerful generative priors of the pretrained backbone, we implement CA3 as a parallel branch alongside the attention layers as illustrated in Fig. 2-(b). For each transformer block ℓ\ell, the hidden state 𝐡ℓ\mathbf{h}_{\ell} is updated as:

𝐡ℓ′=𝐡ℓ+𝒜ℓself​(𝐡ℓ)+𝒜ℓcam​(𝐡ℓ,{𝐏(n)}n=1N),\mathbf{h}^{\prime}_{\ell}=\mathbf{h}_{\ell}+\mathcal{A}^{\text{self}}_{\ell}(\mathbf{h}_{\ell})+\mathcal{A}^{\text{cam}}_{\ell}(\mathbf{h}_{\ell},\{\mathbf{P}^{(n)}\}_{n=1}^{N}), (6)

where 𝒜ℓself(.)\mathcal{A}^{\text{self}}_{\ell}(.) is LoRA-adapted backbone self-attention and 𝒜ℓcam(.,.)\mathcal{A}^{\text{cam}}_{\ell}(.,.) is our trainable camera adapter that uses the projective matrices of the views. To maintain computational efficiency, each adapter employs an 8×8\times dimensionality bottleneck (1536→1921536\to 192) and utilizes only H′=2H^{\prime}{=}2 attention heads, and its output projection is zero-initialised [56] to preserve the pretrained prior at the start of training. The adapter architecture above addresses where to attend across views; however, the backbone features themselves must also be adapted to the sketch domain.

Sketch-Domain Adaptation via LoRA. The video backbone is pretrained exclusively on natural videos; freehand sketches represent a significant domain shift that the camera adapters alone cannot bridge. We therefore apply LoRA [15] with rank 16 to the query, key, value, and output projections of the backbone’s self-attention layers. While CA3 provides explicit geometric viewpoint control via PRoPE, LoRA handles the complementary task of adapting the backbone’s feature representations for sketch-conditioned generation. Training follows a curriculum that lets domain adaptation stabilise before geometric supervision is introduced (Sec. 3.4). We validate this design choice in Sec. 4.3.

3.4 Correspondence Supervision Loss (CSL)

The camera adapters give the model the capacity to distinguish viewpoints, but this geometric inductive bias alone does not teach the model which spatial locations across views correspond to the same 3D point. Without explicit supervision, the adapter’s attention remains diffuse and spatially unstructured, as we verify empirically in Sec. 4.4. We therefore introduce CSL derived from SfM that directly teaches cross-view geometric reasoning (Fig. 4).

Correspondence Extraction. Given the pseudo ground-truth multi-view images for each training sample, we run COLMAP [39] to obtain sparse 3D reconstructions. For each reconstructed 3D point 𝐗j\mathbf{X}_{j}, COLMAP provides its projection coordinates (uj(n),vj(n))(u^{(n)}_{j},v^{(n)}_{j}) in each observing view nn, along with a confidence score cj(n)c^{(n)}_{j} derived from reprojection error. We construct pairwise supervision targets:

𝒞={(qi,ki,wi)}i=1M,\mathcal{C}=\{(q_{i},k_{i},w_{i})\}_{i=1}^{M},

where MM is the total number of correspondence pairs, qi=(nq,sq)q_{i}=(n_{q},s_{q}) and ki=(nk,sk)k_{i}=(n_{k},s_{k}) specify the (view index, spatial patch index) for each pair and wi=min⁡(cj(nq),cj(nk))w_{i}=\min(c^{(n_{q})}_{j},c^{(n_{k})}_{j}) is the confidence weight.

Sparse InfoNCE loss. Directly supervising the full attention matrix 𝐀(ℓ)∈ℝT×T\mathbf{A}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times T} is memory-prohibitive (T>29,000T>29{,}000). We instead formulate correspondence supervision as a contrastive objective on the adapter’s query and key projections. For each correspondence pair (qi,ki)(q_{i},k_{i}), we extract query and key embeddings 𝐪i\mathbf{q}_{i} and 𝐤i\mathbf{k}_{i} from the CA3 module at a subset of layers 𝒰={10,15,20,25}\mathcal{U}=\{10,15,20,25\}, corresponding to middle-to-deep layers where geometric reasoning is most pronounced. The sparse InfoNCE loss is:

ℒcorr=−1M∑i=1Mwi⋅logexp⁡(𝐪i⊤​𝐤i+/τ)exp⁡(𝐪i⊤​𝐤i+/τ)+∑j=1Nnegexp⁡(𝐪i⊤​𝐤j−/τ),\mathcal{L}_{\text{corr}}=-\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}w_{i}\cdot\log\frac{\exp(\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{i}^{+}/\tau)}{\exp(\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{i}^{+}/\tau)+\sum_{j=1}^{N_{\text{neg}}}\exp(\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{j}^{-}/\tau)},

where 𝐤i+\mathbf{k}_{i}^{+} is the positive (corresponding) key, {𝐤j−}j=1Nneg\{\mathbf{k}_{j}^{-}\}_{j=1}^{N_{\text{neg}}} are negative keys sampled from non-corresponding token positions, and τ\tau is a temperature parameter. This formulation has complexity O⁡(M×Nneg)O(M\times N_{\text{neg}}) rather than O⁡(T2)O(T^{2}), reducing memory from 14 GB to ∼{\sim}1 MB.

Total training objective. The final training objective combines the flow matching loss with correspondence supervision:

ℒtotal=ℒflow+λcorr⋅ℒcorr,\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{flow}}+\lambda_{\text{corr}}\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{corr}},

where λcorr\lambda_{\text{corr}} follows a curriculum schedule: it is held at zero during an initial warmup phase, then linearly ramped to its target value of 0.010.01. This allows the flow matching loss and LoRA domain adaptation to stabilise before correspondence supervision is introduced.

4 Experiments

We evaluate our method on sketch-to-multiview generation, assessing both per-view image quality and cross-view geometric consistency. We describe the experimental setup (Sec. 4.1), compare against two strong baselines (Sec. 4.2), present ablations (Sec. 4.3), visualise learned attention (Sec. 4.4), and test generalisation to unseen sketch domains (Sec. 4.5).

4.1 Experimental Setup

Dataset and splits. We train on our S2MV dataset described in Sec. 3.2 with a total of 9,222 sketch–multiview samples (N=33N=33 views each). We split these into 8,304 training, 441 validation, and 477 test samples, following [5]. All reported metrics are computed on the test set across 3 seeds.

Evaluation metrics. We report standard per-view image quality metrics against ground-truth views: peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR↑\uparrow), structural similarity index (SSIM↑\uparrow) [49], and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS↓\downarrow) [57] using an AlexNet backbone. To measure distributional realism, we report FID↓\downarrow [14] computed over all generated views versus all ground-truth views. For semantic fidelity, we compute CLIP-I↑\uparrow (cosine similarity between CLIP ViT-B/32 embeddings of generated and GT views). We additionally report Corr-Acc↑\uparrow, a geometric consistency metric that measures the percentage of COLMAP correspondences whose reprojection error on generated views falls below a threshold of 5 pixels; directly evaluating whether the model preserves the 3D structure visible in ground truth. All per-view metrics are averaged across views, seeds and test samples.

Baselines. No prior method generates geometrically consistent multi-view output from a single freehand scene sketch. Therefore, we evaluate two state-of-the-art novel-view synthesis methods adapted to our setting via a shared two-stage pipeline: FLUX.2-dev [22] first translates each sketch to a photorealistic front view, then either SEVA [60] (Plücker-conditioned latent diffusion, 576×576576\times 576) or ViewCrafter [54] (point-cloud-guided video diffusion via DUSt3R [48], 576×1024576\times 1024) generates the remaining views. Full baseline configurations are provided in the supplementary material (Appendix 0.C).

Implementation details. We set N=33N{=}33 views at 480×480480\times 480 resolution, building on the Wan 2.1 video DiT (1.3B parameters) [45] with frame replication (N→4​N+1N\to 4N{+}1). We train on 8×8\times NVIDIA A100 GPUs with AdamW [33], LoRA [15] rank 16 (∼{\sim}5.9M parameters) alongside ∼{\sim}35.4M CA3 parameters. The correspondence loss follows a curriculum schedule, ramping λcorr\lambda_{\text{corr}} from 00 to 0.010.01. Extended training details are provided in the supplementary material (Appendix 0.B).

4.2 Comparison with Baselines

Quantitative results. Tab. 1 presents the main comparison across all metrics. Our single-stage method outperforms both two-stage baselines on five of six metrics despite operating directly from sketches without an intermediate photorealistic reference. The improvement is most pronounced on realism (FID 18.4918.49 vs. 4646–4848) and geometric consistency (Corr-Acc 0.1990.199 vs. 0.1610.161/0.1360.136), confirming that CA3 and CSL produce views that are individually plausible and mutually coherent. Perceptual quality likewise favours our method (LPIPS 0.6320.632 vs. 0.7050.705/0.7370.737), as does semantic alignment with ground truth (CLIP-I 0.8280.828 vs. 0.7560.756/0.7730.773). ViewCrafter achieves the highest SSIM (0.3380.338), which we attribute to its tendency to produce smoother, lower-frequency outputs that score well on pixel-level structural similarity despite worse perceptual fidelity.

Our single-stage design also provides a 42×42\times inference speedup over ViewCrafter and 3.7×3.7\times over SEVA. More details in the supplementary material (Appendix 0.E).

Qualitative comparison. Fig. 5 presents visual comparisons for representative test sketches. We visualize more examples in the supplementary material (Appendix 0.A).

4.3 Ablation Study

We ablate each component under identical training settings and report results on the S2MV test set averaged across 3 seeds (Tab. 2).

  • •

    CSL (Tab. 2b). Removing the correspondence loss (λcorr=0\lambda_{\text{corr}}{=}0) retains geometric capacity but removes explicit supervision. Row (b) shows the largest Corr-Acc drop among non-catastrophic ablations (0.1750.175 vs. 0.1990.199) and degraded LPIPS (0.6640.664 vs. 0.6320.632), confirming that CSL is essential for translating adapter capacity into cross-view consistency.

  • •

    CA3 (Tab. 2c). Without our CA3 camera adapter, the model has no mechanism to distinguish viewpoints. Row (c) is nearly catastrophic: PSNR drops to 5.0265.026, FID degrades to 266.06266.06, and CLIP-I drops to 0.6320.632, confirming that LoRA alone is insufficient for the multi-view setting.

  • •

    LoRA (Tab. 2d). Row (d) is competitive on per-view quality (PSNR 12.21112.211, FID 19.2719.27), suggesting our CA3 carry most of the representational burden. However, Corr-Acc drops to 0.1880.188, indicating that LoRA’s domain adaptation complements the adapters for fine-grained geometric consistency.

  • •

    Frame replication (Tab. 2e). Without frame replication, the VAE’s 4×4\times temporal compression merges neighbouring views into shared latent frames. Per-view PSNR remains competitive (12.19812.198), but FID more than doubles (42.5442.54 vs. 18.4918.49) and Corr-Acc degrades to 0.1740.174, confirming that preserving view identity through the VAE bottleneck is critical.

Taken together, all components are mutually reinforcing: removing any one degrades geometric consistency.

4.4 Geometric Consistency Evaluation

To understand how correspondence supervision shapes attention, we visualise camera attention maps at layer 20 (Fig. 6). Given a query pixel in the front view, we extract attention weights over three target views at varying viewpoints. With correspondence supervision, attention concentrates sharply on the geometrically correct region, even for the challenging 180∘180^{\circ} back view. Without it (ablation row b), attention is diffuse and spatially unstructured, confirming that CSL directly teaches the adapters where to attend.

4.5 Generalisation to Unseen Sketch Domains

Our model is trained exclusively on FS-COCO freehand sketches. To test whether the learned geometric reasoning transfers to unseen sketch distributions or not, we evaluate on sketches from two out-of-distribution datasets (see Appendix 0.D in supplementary) and the qualitative results are illustrated in Fig. 7. From these results, it is clear that per-view image quality and consistency between multi-views are plausible, even if the data distributions are different than FS-COCO.

4.6 Limitations

Our method has some limitations: (i) limited training scale (8 3048\,304 samples vs. >1>1M for baselines), which restricts scene diversity; (ii) generated rather than rendered ground truth, inheriting subtle artefacts from the editing model; and (iii) 480×480480\times 480 resolution, constrained by GPU memory for NN simultaneous views. We provide a detailed discussion in the supplementary material (Appendix 0.F).

5 Conclusion

We presented the first method to generate geometrically consistent multi-view scenes from a single freehand sketch in one forward pass, unifying a curated S2MV dataset, lightweight parallel CA3, and a sparse CSL into three mutually reinforcing components. Beyond multi-view synthesis, we believe this opens a broader direction: sketching as a lightweight, accessible interface for 3D content creation. More generally, our work demonstrates that combining camera-aware attention adapters with explicit correspondence supervision is an effective paradigm for lifting 2D generative models into geometrically grounded multi-view generators.

Supplementary Material

This supplementary document provides additional details that complement the main paper. Appendix 0.A presents additional qualitative comparisons. Appendix 0.B gives extended implementation details including gradient flow, training configuration, and correspondence sampling. Appendix 0.C describes the baseline configurations used for evaluation. Appendix 0.E reports inference efficiency comparisons. Appendix 0.F provides an extended discussion of limitations.

Interactive HTML viewer. We include an interactive viewer in the supplementary zip file at supp_vis/index.html. Open it in any browser to browse 50 test samples side-by-side across methods (Ours, SEVA, ViewCrafter) compared to ground truth views. The viewer supports filtering by elevation (0∘0^{\circ}, ±30∘\pm 30^{\circ}, +60∘+60^{\circ}) and displays the input sketch with its caption alongside the generated views. No internet connection or installation is required.
